articles.title: Self-driving test fleets are quietly leaving their pilot cities
articles.subtitle: The expansion nobody announced with a press release
articles.excerpt: Autonomous test fleets that spent years confined to a handful of pilot cities are now showing up in new metro areas with far less fanfare.
articles.author: admin

content.text: For years, autonomous test fleets stayed confined to a small handful of sunbelt cities with wide roads and predictable weather. That's changing quietly, without the launch events that accompanied earlier expansions.
New markets, less noise
Regulatory filings show permit applications in several colder, denser cities that were previously considered too difficult for current-generation systems.
Operators say the quieter approach is deliberate, avoiding the scrutiny that came with earlier high-profile launches while the safety record in new conditions is still being established.

articles.title: Why highway charging stations still feel like the 1990s
articles.subtitle: Hardware improved. The waiting experience didn't.
articles.excerpt: Charging speeds have gone up year over year, but the actual experience of stopping at a highway charger hasn't caught up.
articles.author: ashraf

content.text: Peak charging speeds have roughly doubled at many highway sites over the last three years. Ask any driver what actually changed about the stop itself, though, and the answer is usually: not much.
The real bottleneck
Payment systems, stall availability during peak travel weekends, and inconsistent signage across networks remain the most common complaints in driver surveys, ahead of raw charging speed.
Some operators are starting to treat charging stops as a hospitality problem rather than a purely electrical one, adding seating and food options alongside the chargers themselves.

articles.title: The used EV market is finally becoming normal
articles.subtitle: Prices are dropping and buyers are less nervous
articles.excerpt: Battery degradation fears kept resale values volatile for years. New data suggests the used electric vehicle market is stabilizing.
articles.author: ashraf

content.text: Overview
Battery degradation fears kept resale values volatile for years. New data suggests the used electric vehicle market is stabilizing.
Prices are dropping and buyers are less nervous

Prices are dropping and buyers are less nervous. Battery degradation fears kept resale values volatile for years, but new data suggests the used electric vehicle market is stabilizing, with month-to-month price swings down to about 2% compared to over 8% two years ago.
Independent battery health checks are a big part of that shift — listings that include a verified state-of-health report now sell in roughly half the time of comparable listings without one.
What buyers should check

items: Request a battery state-of-health report, not just a mileage figure
Check whether the battery warranty transfers to a second owner
Compare DC fast-charging speed against the original spec sheet

content.text: Financing is catching up too: several major lenders now offer the same loan terms for used EVs as for comparable gas vehicles, something that was rare even 18 months ago.
Our take

It's an encouraging sign for where the category is headed next, even if not every question has been answered yet — long-term battery replacement costs are still the biggest unknown for buyers going past year eight.

articles.title: Solid-state batteries just left the lab for the first time
articles.subtitle: A decade of promises meets a real production timeline
articles.excerpt: After years of demos that never left the lab, a solid-state battery is finally headed to a production line.
articles.author: admin

content.text: Solid-state batteries have been described as "five years away" for most of the last decade. That changes with a supplier confirming a pilot production line is now running, not just a lab bench demo.
Why it matters

The pitch has always been faster charging and a lighter pack for the same range. The open question was whether the manufacturing process could scale past a handful of prototype cells, which is the part this milestone actually addresses.
Early production volumes are small, and the first cars to use the new cells aren't expected on sale for at least two more years.

articles.title: Of course Uber is working on a flying car project
articles.subtitle: The Surface Book 2 this isn't
articles.excerpt: For a slightly more opinionated version of the video review above, here's the male half of the team arguing about whether this device is a great or a terrible product.
articles.author: admin

content.text: Design

The device is beautifully designed and engineered, with a great look and feel. Its chunky, rounded body is faintly reminiscent of earlier generations, yet simultaneously modern-looking and very satisfying to hold. It is also pleasingly comfortable to carry.

We have seen lots of trackers over the years, and they have typically struck us as pretty formulaic: plasticky wristbands with little fashion appeal. One brand tried to convince us that their tracker was designed to appeal to a fashion-conscious buyer; they even suggested people would wear it as jewellery. But at the end of the day, it wasn't jewellery. None of the trackers on the market are.
Dimensions
There are two sizes available: a compact model and a larger model. Both share the same thickness, keeping the design consistent across the range.
Build quality

Speaking of the materials used, there are three tiers: an aluminium sport option, a stainless steel standard option, and an 18-carat gold premium edition. The standard and premium versions come with sapphire-coated screens, while the sport version uses ion-x glass.
We love the look and feel of this device — it's reassuringly robust.

Manufacturer guidance recommends caution around water exposure. While the device is rated water-resistant to a reasonable standard, it is described as splash- and water-resistant rather than fully waterproof, so day-to-day exposure to rain or sweat should be fine, but submersion is not recommended.
Straps
There is a wide collection of strap and accessory options to choose from, including several colourways and materials to suit different tastes and budgets.
Screen

The resolution depends on the model you choose. Both models offer a comparable pixel density, and the screen quality is excellent across the range — sharp, vividly colourful, with no noticeable pixellation even under close inspection.
User interface
The interface is intuitive once you get used to the gesture system. Elements are sized appropriately for touch input, avoiding the common problem of tiny UI targets on a small display.
Speed/performance
Performance has generally been solid in our testing, though third-party software can occasionally feel sluggish to launch. Native features remain snappy throughout.
Battery life
Typical usage should get you through a full day of moderate use. Heavier workloads such as continuous media playback or workout tracking will reduce this somewhat, so plan to charge overnight.
Pricing and availability
Pricing varies depending on the configuration and accessories you choose, with the entry-level sport configuration offering the best value for most buyers.
Our verdict

This isn't the first product of its kind, and it doesn't really do anything rival products don't do. But what it does do, it does well, thanks to strong interface design. It's a slick product to use, although it isn't completely intuitive at first — with use it becomes more familiar.

commentsList.name: Jae-won L.
commentsList.text: Disagree a bit on the middle section, but the overall conclusion tracks with my own experience.

articles.title: The spare tire is quietly disappearing from new cars
articles.subtitle: Weight savings win out over roadside convenience
articles.excerpt: Automakers are swapping full-size spares for inflation kits and run-flat tires, trading a rare inconvenience for meaningful gains in fuel economy and cargo space.
articles.author: admin

content.text: Overview
Automakers are swapping full-size spares for inflation kits and run-flat tires, trading a rare inconvenience for meaningful gains in fuel economy and cargo space.
Why this is happening now
A full-size spare and jack assembly can add over 40 pounds to a vehicle, a meaningful chunk of the weight budget automakers are chasing to hit emissions targets.
Roadside assistance coverage has also become close to universal, reducing the practical downside of not carrying a full spare.
Our take
It's a reasonable trade-off for most drivers, though it's worth checking what your specific car includes before a long road trip.
